title: Negative quasiprobabilities redistribute (and complex ones reduce) the information in unabsorbed photons
abstract: Negative Kirkwood--Dirac quasiprobabilities are credited with the quantum advantage of interaction-free measurement and postselected metrology. We test that claim on the task interaction-free measurement was designed for: learning about a sample letting it absorb as little light as possible. The Kirkwood--Dirac distribution of path and output gives the linear response to a weak sample: its real part responds to absorption, its imaginary part to a phase. For a pure single photon passing once through any interferometer, the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon is the direct-transmission value minus a sum of squared imaginary parts: no interferometer or readout beats direct transmission. Negativity plays no role beyond concentrating information in weakly lit outputs. The imaginary parts of the Kirkwood-Dirac distribution depend on the output basis here, not on the sample, so a basis exists in which every term is real, which is optimal. A single photon gains information per absorbed photon only through a phase response, which for an optical line needs a thick or inhomogeneously broadened sample, or through many passes when absorptions go uncounted, as shown by a critically coupled resonator. For detecting a weak absorber, negativity gives a single-shot advantage that does not accumulate over multiple trials; advantage instead accumulates when there are outputs which are dark without the object, a case which needs no negativity.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the information content gained from measuring a weak absorber using single photons in an interferometer. It demonstrates that while negative quasiprobabilities are theoretically significant, they do not improve the information per absorbed photon in a single pass. True advantages are found either through phase accumulation over multiple passes or when the measurement setup is designed to exploit specific interference effects.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental limits on the information gain per absorbed photon when performing interaction-free measurements on a weak sample.
main_result: For single-pass measurements, negativity does not improve the total information per absorbed photon; advantage only accumulates over multiple, uncounted passes or when the phase response is significant.
method: The analysis uses the Fisher information derived from the linear response of output probabilities to weak absorption or phase shifts, utilizing negative Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities.
model_or_system: The system models a single photon passing through a $d$-path interferometer containing a weak absorber with transmittance $t$. The analysis extends to multi-pass scenarios using ring resonators.
key_observables: Fisher information ($F_s(t)$), evidence per absorbed photon ($\eta$), and the complex Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities ($\varrho_C$).
important_parameters: Transmittance $t$, number of passes $\ell$, and the weak value $\langle\hat{\Pi}(a)angle_w$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations, such as the Gaussian regime or small probabilities of absorption ($P(a)$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the interferometer setup, showing how the single-shot gain ($R_M^{-1}$) decays for different measurement limits and how the gain is enhanced by negative weak values near null ports.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the single-pass bound using Fisher information (Theorem 1) to analyzing the role of negativity, and finally extends the analysis to multi-pass systems and the evidence gain ($\eta$) using advanced entropy measures.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical bounds on quantum metrology, specifically quantifying when and how negative quasiprobabilities can enhance measurement sensitivity beyond classical limits in the context of photon loss.
